lines: The particular person is already fixed at position {fixedPosition}, so that place contributes no further choice.
Only the remaining {remainingObjects} people need to be arranged in the remaining positions.
The count is {equation}, giving {answer} arrangements.
Choose whether the particular person stands at the left end or the right end.
After that end is fixed, arrange all remaining people freely in the other places.
Thus {equation}, so the required number is {answer}.
The two particular people occupy the two ends and may exchange those end positions.
Once the ends are filled, arrange the remaining {remainingObjects} people in the middle positions.
This gives {equation}, or {answer} arrangements.
The particular person may use any position except the two ends, leaving {allowedPositionCount} allowed places.
For each such position, arrange the other people in the remaining places.
The calculation {equation} gives {answer} valid rows.
Every arrangement has a matching arrangement obtained by swapping A and B.
Exactly one arrangement in each matched pair has A before B, so half of all arrangements qualify.
Therefore {equation}, which gives {answer} arrangements.
Ignore where the three specified files occur and focus only on their internal order.
Their positions permit all \(3!\) relative orders equally often, and only A-before-B-before-C is accepted.
Hence {equation}, giving {answer} arrangements.
The four specified tasks can occupy their chosen places in \(4!\) possible relative orders.
Only one of those internal orders is prescribed, while all other tasks remain unrestricted.
Dividing by that order factor gives {equation}, so the answer is {answer}.
The condition A before B removes half of all arrangements, and the independent condition C before D removes half again.
Equivalently, divide the unrestricted count by the two order factors \(2!\) and \(2!\).
Using {equation}, both conditions hold in {answer} arrangements.
With equal group sizes, an alternating row may start with either a boy or a girl.
For each of those two patterns, arrange the boys in their slots and the girls in theirs.
So {equation}, producing {answer} alternating rows.
Because the boys outnumber the girls by one, strict alternation forces a boy at both ends.
That leaves one category pattern; arrange the boys in the boy-slots and the girls in the girl-slots.
The count {equation} equals {answer}.
The first-position colour fixes which of the two equal-category alternating patterns is allowed.
Arrange the red cards in the red slots and the blue cards in the blue slots.
This gives {equation}, so there are {answer} arrangements.
Arrange the {largeCount} men first; they create {gapSlotCount} gaps, including the two end gaps.
Choose {smallCount} different gaps for the women so that no gap receives two women, then arrange the women within those chosen gaps.
The resulting count is {equation}, giving {answer} rows.
First arrange the {largeCount} people outside the specified set; this creates {gapSlotCount} safe gaps.
Place the {specifiedCount} specified people in different gaps and arrange them, which prevents any two from becoming adjacent.
Thus {equation}, and the number of valid arrangements is {answer}.
The two particular people must occupy positions separated by exactly {gapCount} intervening places.
There are {orderedPositionPairCount} ordered choices for their positions, after which the other people fill the remaining places freely.
Therefore {equation}, giving {answer} arrangements.
Allow every ordered pair of positions whose separation leaves at least {minimumGap} people between the two particular people.
Those acceptable separations provide {orderedPositionPairCount} ordered position pairs, and the remaining people can then be arranged freely.
The calculation is {equation}, so {answer} arrangements qualify.
There are {eligibleClassPositions} even-numbered positions available for the {specifiedCount} specified books.
Assign the specified books to distinct eligible positions, then arrange every remaining book in the unfilled positions.
This produces {equation}, or {answer} arrangements.
Choose which {requiredInClass} of the {specifiedCount} specified people occupy odd-numbered positions.
Assign them to odd positions, assign the remaining specified people to even positions, and then arrange all ordinary people in the unused places.
Combining those stages gives {equation}, so the answer is {answer}.
Evaluate the exact-gap count for each allowed positive value of \(d\).
Only one candidate produces the target {target}; its verified equation is {equation}.
Hence the required number of people between the specified pair is {answer}.
